content_voiceover: The gel card, or column agglutination technique, works by physically trapping agglutinated cells in a gel matrix. Each microtube contains red cells, antibodies or antiserum, and a gel or glass bead matrix. After incubation and centrifugation, agglutinated red cells are too large to pass through the gel and stay trapped near the top, giving a positive reaction, while unagglutinated single cells pass all the way through to the bottom, giving a negative reaction. In this example, the blood typing card shows anti-A 4 plus, anti-B negative, anti-D 4 plus, confirming type A, Rh positive, matching what we saw with the tube method. The antibody screen card, using screening cells one, two, and three coated with IgG, shows all negative results here. The workflow is simple: load cells and antiserum into the reaction chamber, sometimes preloaded like anti-A, anti-B, or AHG; centrifuge, letting the gel or beads block agglutinated cells while unagglutinated cells pass through; then grade the reaction from zero to 4 plus based on how far the cells travelled.
keypoints: Gel card traps agglutinated RBCs in gel matrix; unagglutinated cells pass through to the bottom.
Agglutinated cells near top mean positive; cells at bottom mean negative.
Reagents like anti-A, anti-B, and AHG are often preloaded in gel card columns.
Reactions graded 0 to 4+ based on position or spread of cells after centrifugation.
